summary: The note traces the history of the Catholic rosary devotion. It covers its official establishment by Pope Pius V's 1569 papal bull, the advocacy of Saint Peter Canisius, and the structure of mysteries and prayers that stayed largely unchanged until 2002. It also notes the rosary's prominence in Marian art and in churches named after it.
one_line: History of the Catholic rosary, from its 1569 papal establishment through later structural changes and its role in Marian art and churches.
key_facts: In 1569, the papal bull Consueverunt Romani Pontifices by the Dominican Pope Pius V officially established the devotion to the rosary in the Catholic Church.
Saint Peter Canisius, a Doctor of the Church, is credited with adding to the Hail Mary the sentence "Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners".
Saint Peter Canisius promoted the rosary and Marian devotion as the best way to repair the damage done to the Church by the Reformation.
From the 16th to the early 20th century, the structure of the rosary remained essentially unchanged, with 15 mysteries, one for each of the 15 decades.
In the 20th century, the addition of the Fatima Prayer to the end of each decade became popular.
After Vatican Council II, Msgr. Annibale Bugnini, architect of the liturgical reform, proposed further changes to the structure of the Rosary.

Pope Paul VI refused to implement Bugnini's proposal, reasoning that changing such a well-established and popular devotion would unsettle the piety of the faithful and show a lack of reverence for an ancient practice.
In 2002, John Paul II instituted five new Luminous Mysteries, the first structural change after Paul VI's refusal.
In the 17th century, the Rosary began to appear as an element in key pieces of Roman Catholic Marian art.
Murillo's Madonna with the Rosary is held at the Museo del Prado in Spain.
A statue of Madonna with Rosary stands at the church of San Nazaro Maggiore in Milan.
Several Roman Catholic Marian churches are named after the rosary, including Our Lady of the Rosary Basilica in Rosario, Argentina.
The Rosary Basilica in Lourdes and Nossa Senhora do Rosário in Porto Alegre, Brazil are also named after the rosary.
